note: Rewritten to the claim that survived the four independent audits.

problems.original_statement: A per-protocol effect requires censoring at deviation and weighting for the informative censoring that censoring creates. Beneath that mechanics sits a question the mechanics assume away: what counts as the same treatment. Real treatments differ by dose, route, provider, formulation, combination and adherence pattern, and two regimens sharing a label may not satisfy consistency. Clone-censor-weight handles the case where baseline assignment is genuinely ambiguous, at the cost of data expansion, artificial censoring and sensitivity to the censoring model, but it takes the strategy definition as given. There is no guidance for constructing defensible equivalence classes of treatment versions, and none for overlapping combination therapies where a patient is simultaneously compatible with more than one labeled strategy.
problems.correction_note: Three corrections. Artificial censoring with inverse probability weighting is one valid way to estimate a per-protocol effect, not a requirement. Clone-censor-weight does handle individuals compatible with several predefined strategies, which the entry listed as unaddressed; what it does not do is decide whether treatment versions should be pooled. And observed data can expose heterogeneity across versions even though they cannot establish that versions are irrelevant, so the situation is not entirely uninformative.
problems.statement: Estimating a per-protocol effect requires the sustained strategy and its relevant treatment versions to be clinically specified first; artificial censoring with inverse probability weighting is one valid estimation route rather than a requirement. Beneath the mechanics sits the question the mechanics assume answered: what counts as the same treatment. Real treatments differ by dose, route, provider, formulation, combination and adherence pattern, and two regimens sharing a label may not satisfy consistency. Clone-censor-weight handles a patient compatible with several predefined strategies and does not decide whether versions should be pooled into one. Observed data can expose heterogeneity across versions and cannot establish that versions are irrelevant, so the pooling decision is clinical. Finer definitions also create practical support problems, so the more faithful specification is often the less identifiable one, and no guidance exists for making that trade.
problems.why_open: Consistency is an assumption about the world rather than about the data, so no amount of data adjudicates whether two versions are the same treatment; heterogeneity across versions is evidence against pooling and its absence is not evidence for it. The clinical judgment that would adjudicate is specific to the drug, the indication and the era, which makes a general criterion the wrong shape. And making the versions explicit multiplies the strategies, each costing positivity, so the honest specification is frequently the one the data cannot support.
problems.proposed_direction: Use hierarchical treatment ontologies and latent treatment-version models so the equivalence class is an explicit, versioned object, and report the observed heterogeneity across versions as evidence bearing on the pooling decision rather than as a robustness check. Estimate joint effects of initiation, dose and adherence through longitudinal multivariate modified treatment policies where an analyst-specified joint policy is what is wanted, noting that such an estimator does not supply the equivalence classes and need not target the same per-protocol estimand. Quantify by simulation how much bias a wrong equivalence class induces relative to the positivity cost of the correct one, since that trade is the actual decision.
